extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent owners, third-party challengers, and IP professionals interested in U.S. re-examination and PTAB proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria governing ex parte re-examination and inter partes review (IPR) in U.S. patent law, including eligibility, required contents, thresholds for institution, timelines, allowable actions, appeal rights, and related judicial and PTO developments. Useful for parties considering or responding to re-exam or IPR petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of re-examination available
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of re-examination mechanisms exist in U.S. patent law: ex parte re-examination (codified at 35 U.S.C. §§ 302-307) and inter partes review (codified at 35 U.S.C. §§ 311-319).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ex parte re-examination is the older statutory mechanism (enacted 1980) to resolve validity disputes via the USPTO; inter partes review was introduced by the AIA (effective Sept 16, 2012) and is conducted by the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte re-examination — who may file and required contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Any person, including the patent owner, may file a request for ex parte re-examination by providing a written request accompanied by the fee, the pertinent prior art, and the manner of applying the prior art to the claim(s) at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An attorney may file on behalf of a real party in interest to keep that party's identity confidential. The requester must supply patents or printed publications as prior art (35 U.S.C. § 302).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte re-examination — permissible prior art and USPTO scope of consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art submitted by the requester must consist of patents or printed publications, but the USPTO is not limited to the prior art submitted by the requester and may consider other patents and printed publications in the file.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant prior art included in the official file under 35 U.S.C. § 301 may be considered; third-party-submitted art that becomes part of the file can be considered in the re-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte re-examination — USPTO threshold determination (substantial new question) and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will determine within three months whether the request raises a 'substantial new question of patentability' affecting any claim, and if so, will initiate re-examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO's determination that no substantial new question has been raised is final and non-appealable by either party (i.e., no appeal from denial of re-exam institution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and criteria for a 'substantial new question of patentability' (SNQ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art patent or printed publication raises an SNQ where there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable examiner would consider the prior art important in deciding whether the claim is patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SNQ requires that (i) the prior art raises a substantial question of patentability regarding at least one claim (i.e., a reasonable examiner would find it important), and (ii) the same question has not been decided previously by the Office or by a final holding of invalidity on the merits. The submitted art need not form a prima facie case; cumulative art does not create an SNQ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte re-examination — patent owner opportunity and third-party response
rubrics_metrics.description: If the USPTO orders re-examination, the patent owner is given not less than two months from the date the determination copy is given to file a statement including any proposed amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of the owner's statement is communicated to the requester, who may submit a response. If the owner elects not to file a statement, the requester may not file any further communications in the proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte re-examination — conduct and scope of amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: After initial time limits expire, the re-examination is conducted similarly to the initial examination. The patent owner may propose any amendment and may add a new claim to distinguish over cited prior art, but the scope of the claims may not be enlarged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure mirrors initial examination practice; amendments must not broaden the claim scope beyond the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ex parte re-examination — appeals and participation rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the USPTO renders a decision in re-examination, the patent owner may appeal an adverse determination to the Board of Patent Appeals and Interferences (BPAI) and further to the Federal Circuit or District Court; the original ex parte requester (if not the owner) has no right to participate in these appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requester (other than the patent owner) cannot participate in appeals from ex parte re-exam decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — statutory scope of challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter partes review (IPR) reviews the patentability of one or more patent claims only on grounds that could be raised under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 or 103 (novelty and non-obviousness), and only on the basis of prior art consisting of patents or printed publications (35 U.S.C. § 311).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other grounds outside 102/103 are not available in IPR; testimonial evidence alone is insufficient — the basis must be patents/printed publications (though affidavits/declarations may support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — timing limits to file a petition
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for IPR must be filed after the later of (1) nine months after grant of the patent or issuance of a reissue patent, or (2) if a post-grant review is instituted, the termination of the post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain circumstances bar institution: if the petitioner filed a civil action challenging the validity of a claim before filing the petition, or if the petition is filed more than one year after the petitioner was served with a complaint alleging infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — petition contents and public availability
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must be based on copies of patents and printed publications, affidavits or declarations of supporting evidence, or other documents, and the petition will be made available to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because petitions are public, strategic and confidentiality considerations are important when deciding whether to file or submit supporting documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — institution standard (reasonable likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: To institute an IPR, it is necessary to show that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least one claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director's threshold determination on institution is not appealable; this is analogous to the institution stage in other post-grant proceedings (see 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — timing and appeal of final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: If instituted and not dismissed, the Board must issue a final determination within one year, extendable up to six months; the final decision of the Board may be appealed to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-year clock (with limited extension) governs case schedule; parties may seek rehearing at the Board and appeal final written decisions to the Federal Circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — estoppel and litigation stay rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules for estoppel (preclusion of issues/arguments in later proceedings) and the stay of civil litigation in IPR are similar to those applicable in post-grant review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instituting an IPR can create estoppel consequences for the petitioner and can affect concurrent district court litigation (stays), so consider strategic litigation impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter partes review — conduct of proceedings and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The conduct of IPR is similar to post-grant review and may include oral hearings; if instituted, the PTAB will address the claims and issue a final written decision on patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR proceedings are adversarial administrative trials before the PTAB with evidence, briefs, and typically an oral hearing; the Board's final written decision resolves patentability issues subject to appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial and PTO developments affecting IPR (precedent and Director review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme Court decisions and USPTO Director review processes have shaped IPR practice: the Supreme Court upheld constitutionality of IPR (Oil States) and ruled that instituted IPRs should address all challenged claims (SAS). The USPTO implemented interim Director-review processes post-Arthrex allowing Director review (sua sponte or on party request) of PTAB final written decisions, with revisions in July 2023.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent procedural and jurisdictional developments (Arthrex, Oil States, SAS) affect appealability, Director involvement, and how PTAB decisions are reviewed—practitioners must track USPTO interim processes and case law when planning or responding to IPRs.
